save & checkpoint model and its tension (limited saves, save rooms, ink ribbons, autosave)
inventory & management pressure (slots, the item box, meaningful item choices)
the tension/safety pacing rhythm (dread vs. safe-room relief; the escalation curve)
level/space design as a pressure system (safe-room hubs, backtracking, locked maze maps)

title: The Survivors-like (Auto-Attacking Horde-Survival) Genre
determines: the auto-attack/no-aim-required combat model (movement is the player's only input; weapons fire automatically at nearest/random/strongest targets, shifting skill expression to positioning and build decisions)
the build-snowball/exponential power curve (weapon-evolution and stacking-synergy escalation that must feel like an accelerating avalanche across a single run)
the horde-density escalation curve (enemy count/density increasing on a fixed timer rather than by player action — a clock-driven difficulty ramp independent of player skill)
the pick-3-of-random-upgrades level-up choice architecture (the genre's primary strategic-decision cadence, recurring dozens of times per run)
run length and structure (typically a fixed timer, e.g. ~15-30 minutes (illustrative))
the late-game visual-chaos/readability problem (hundreds of enemies and effects on screen simultaneously, requiring deliberate visual-hierarchy design so the player stays legible)
meta-progression between runs (permanent unlocks/currency sustaining engagement despite short, disposable individual runs)
the build-diversity/replayability engine (dozens of weapons/synergies/evolutions creating build variety as the genre's answer to "why play again")
platform/input fit (the genre's low mechanical-execution demand and its suitability for mobile/touch and short sessions)

title: The Tactical / Milsim Shooter Genre
determines: lethality model (very low TTK / one-shot-down; the deliberate-play causality)
realism systems (ballistics/bullet-drop, recoil, stance/lean, weapon weight & handling, limited HUD, no arcade regen)
teamplay & communication as a mechanic (callouts, roles, covering angles, voice comms, the solo-queue problem)
deliberate pacing model (tense lulls + lethal bursts; clearing/holding; round-based vs respawn)
the plan→breach→execute loop and the prep/setup phase (recon/drones/intel, the gadget/destruction/info meta)
round / objective structure & attack-defend asymmetry
permadeath / no-respawn-in-round stakes and their pacing consequences
tactical map & objective design (CQB layouts, multiple entries, destructible/breachable geometry, sightlines)
hardcore↔accessible tuning (keeping high-lethality tense not frustrating)
sub-form selection (tactical-CQB vs milsim-scale vs tactical-coop/PvE)

title: The Tactical RPG (SRPG) Genre
determines: grid/tile combat model (square vs hex, movement/range/LoS, facing, zones of control, height, damage resolution)
positioning & terrain rules (high ground, cover, flanking, chokepoints, formation, the spatial puzzle)
action-economy structure (moves/actions per turn, action advantage, tempo, initiative/turn order)
unit/class-building & progression (classes/jobs, leveling, equipment, skill synergy, party composition, depth-vs-balance)
information-vs-RNG philosophy & RNG mitigation (perfect-info puzzle vs hit-chance gamble; streak-breakers/graze bands/transparency)
mission & encounter design (objectives beyond elimination, map variety, reinforcements, difficulty, permadeath stakes)
enemy tactical AI (challenge without cheating)

title: The Third-Person Shooter (TPS) Genre
determines: the over-the-shoulder camera framing (shoulder offset, FOV, aim-zoom, occlusion/collision, shoulder-swap)
the cover-system model (sticky/snap vs freeform; peek/blind-fire/vault; cover-to-cover; the cover-shooter grammar)
third-person gunplay feel & the aim model (reticle vs camera-offset, ADS-snap, TTK, hit feedback on a visible target)
movement/traversal/animation-in-combat (roll/dodge, vault, melee, mantle, animation-driven feel and the input-latency trade)
the TPS-vs-FPS trade (awareness/animation/cover-readability/cinematics vs aiming precision/immersion) and when to choose which camera
encounter/arena design around cover layouts, flanking routes, sightlines, and cover-using AI
sub-form selection (cover-shooter / cinematic-action-TPS / over-the-shoulder-survival / TPS-RPG-looter) and its pillars
SP-vs-MP TPS priorities

title: The Tower Defense Genre
determines: the path/map & placement model (fixed-path vs maze-building/open-field vs multi-lane) and how the map constrains placement
tower archetype set & the damage-type/counter (rock-paper-scissors) web
the wave/spawn escalation curve & wave composition (rushes, mixed, boss waves)
the tower economy (gold-per-kill, build-vs-upgrade, interest/eco, sell-back, the power curve)
the fail condition (lives/leaks) and the difficulty tiers/endless-mode structure
difficulty design & the solved-optimal-layout problem and its mitigations
active-vs-passive player agency (hero units, targeting priority, activated abilities, hand-placed spells)
roguelite/meta-progression hybrids (knowledge/upgrade trees, run modifiers) and co-op/competitive modes

title: The Turn-Based Strategy & 4X Genre
determines: the 4X loop as a phase-pacing spine (eXplore → eXpand → eXploit → eXterminate, one X leading each act)
the interacting-subsystem web (economy/production, research/tech + civics, diplomacy, culture/happiness, military, espionage) and its feedback edges
tech & civic tree design and the research economy (beeline vs. broad, era gating, catch-up)
city / tile-yield management and the empire-management burden (tall vs. wide, per-city micro)
the snowball / runaway-leader problem and catch-up / comeback mechanics (per-era catch-up, war-weariness, coalitions, upkeep drag)
victory conditions & asymmetric win-paths (domination / science / culture / diplomatic) and how multiple win rails keep games alive
the "one more turn" compulsion loop (interlocking incomplete progress bars, per-turn reward + next-turn setup)
the late-game slog / endgame micromanagement failure and its mitigations (automation, governors, tempo, turn-count caps)
long-arc pacing across a multi-hour single session (era shape, front-loaded vs. back-loaded interest)
AI design across a huge state space and the bonus-based-difficulty crutch

title: The Twin-Stick Shooter Genre
determines: the dual-analog control scheme (move-and-aim independence as the genre's defining verb) and its input variants (twin-stick / aim-toward-cursor / auto-aim assist / the dodge-roll-dash layer)
the enemy-swarm/horde design (massing enemies with distinct movement/threat roles and telegraphing them so a full omnidirectional screen stays readable)
the projectile-dodging spatial problem (omnidirectional crossfire; reading and threading a screen of threats as the core survival puzzle) and its bullet-density-vs-readability balance
the weapon/build-variety model (single-gun control-purity vs. item-synergy/mutation/gun-sandbox depth) and its role as the replayability engine
the arena/wave/spawn design (single-screen arena vs. scrolling rooms; wave pacing; spawn placement as pressure and readability control)
the twin-stick-roguelite marriage decision (arena-score-survival framing vs. run-based-build framing) and why the core fused with roguelite structure
camera/readability-at-scale design (keeping the omnidirectional screen legible and a hard screen fair)
platform/input fit (the genre's native dual-analog gamepad fit; keyboard-and-mouse aim-toward-cursor variant; the control scheme as the platform-defining constraint)

title: The Vehicle Sim Genre
determines: the fidelity/realism position (arcade → simcade → study-sim) — the single choice that sets everything else

the physics/handling model per domain (flight: lift/drag/stall/trim; driving: weight-transfer/grip/tire; space: Newtonian orbital vs arcade; ground/train: momentum/braking/signaling; naval: displacement/inertia)
the control scheme & peripheral support (HOTAS/yoke/rudder, wheel/pedals/shifter, throttle quadrants; keyboard/gamepad fallbacks and how much they compromise)
instrumentation & systems-management depth (cockpit procedures, checklists, avionics/subsystems — operating vs steering)
the learning curve, assists & onboarding (tutorials, difficulty layers, the "read a real manual" barrier and how to lower it)
the structure layer (free-roam/sandbox flying-for-its-own-sake vs missions/career/economy)
immersion & sensory feedback (VR, force feedback, sound, camera, gauges — feeling the machine)
the niche-hardcore vs accessible-mass-market position (the genre's central fork)
the meditative/"zen journey" register vs the mastery/procedure register

title: The Visual Novel Genre
determines: branching narrative structure (kinetic / single-branch / character-routes / true-route-gated / worldline-gauntlet)
choice & flag systems (immediate vs delayed consequence, affection/route flags, thresholds, the illusion-of-choice honesty problem)
route design & locking (route-lock, true-route gating, branch-and-bottleneck, gauntlet-of-bad-ends)
presentation stack (sprite + expression/pose + background + event CG + text box + voice + BGM + transitions)
text-vs-choice pacing (the rhythm of the text box; when to interrupt reading with a decision)
the kinetic-novel-vs-choice spectrum (how much agency to grant)
mechanical-hybrid selection (investigation/cross-examination, escape-room/deduction, trials, dating-sim stats)
medium-as-mechanic use (saves, route-memory, meta-awareness as narrative devices)
reader-pacing UX (skip/auto/backlog/flowchart/save-anywhere)
endings design (true / good / normal / bad / joke; the gauntlet)

title: The Voxel / Creative Sandbox Genre
determines: the build/place/mine/destroy voxel-manipulation core (the editable grid as the fundamental verb)
the block/material/tool palette and how it scopes what is buildable (small-expressive vs thousands-of-blocks)
procedural world generation & effectively-infinite worlds (chunk streaming, biomes, seeds, caves/ores)
the creative-mode vs survival-mode split (unlimited free expression vs gather-and-earn materials)
emergent creativity & player-expression support (redstone-style logic, contraptions, pixel-art, adventure maps)
the no-fail-state open toy play vs layered goals/progression (the toy-vs-game spectrum)
multiplayer / shared-world building (servers, collaborative & griefing dynamics, permissions)
performance & tech of voxel worlds (meshing, chunk LOD, memory/render cost — illustrative)
the UGC / sharing / showcase culture and the creation-engine-to-platform leap (Roblox/Dreams)
modding & the platform effect (Minecraft mods, Roblox as UGC platform)

title: Interactive Narrative / Walking Simulators
determines: environmental-storytelling design (story told through space/objects/traces — the "archaeology" of a scene)
spatial pacing & exploration-as-pacing (the walk sets the tempo; sightline/landmark guidance; critical-path-vs-optional-detail budget) with no combat/fail-state
the interaction budget ("gameplay is walking / looking / picking-up / triggering") and why minimalism is the point
discovery & delivery-channel design (audio logs, diegetic notes, voiceover/narration, discovered dialogue, visual tableau)
mood/atmosphere as the core product (light, sound, weather — cross-ref visual/audio domains)
pacing without mechanics (curiosity + emotional beats replace challenge)
the critique answer ("is it a game?" / substance-vs-pretension) and how to design past it
length/density calibration (short & dense beats long & hollow)
the variant selection (first-person-exploration vs vignette-anthology vs meta-narrative)

title: The Wargame Genre
determines: the hex-and-counter / operational map model (hexes vs zones/areas, zones-of-control, stacking limits)
the combat-resolution system (CRT/combat-results-table, odds ratios, dice/algorithm, calibrated randomness)
supply/logistics & command-and-control systems (supply lines/depots, out-of-supply attrition, command points, chit-pull/activation)
the scale tier (tactical squad-level vs operational division/corps vs strategic theater) and the turn/impulse structure it implies
fog-of-war / intelligence model (double-blind, limited-intel, spotting)
historical fidelity vs playability balance (OOB accuracy, period stats, history-respecting outcomes)
the complexity/onboarding wall and its digital mitigations (auto-supply, tooltips, tutorials, phased rules)
the turn-based vs real-time-hybrid choice and the solitaire/AI vs PBEM/hotseat play model

title: 3D Look Sensitivity Defaults
determines: the default mouse look sensitivity (degrees of camera rotation per raw mouse count) for a 3D camera, first-person and third-person
the default stick look turn rate (degrees per second at full deflection) for a 3D camera, first-person and third-person
the default stick deadzone (inner plus outer, scaled radial) for 3D look input specifically
the player-facing sensitivity slider range for mouse and stick, anchored to the same source math
whether any acceleration/ramp is applied to raw look input (it is not)

title: Aiming & Aim Assist
determines: the core aim model (hitscan vs. projectile, recoil/spread/bloom shape, ADS vs. hipfire split, time-to-target target)

which aim-assist mechanisms to use (reticle friction/slowdown, rotational/"sticky" magnetism, target snap, bullet magnetism/bullet-bending, hit-cone/hitbox padding, full auto-aim) and where each sits on the subtle-to-strong spectrum
the tuning knobs for each mechanism (strength, target-bubble size/shape, ADS vs. hipfire split, velocity ramp, distance falloff, per-weapon values)
the per-input differentiation policy (controller assist strength vs. mouse assist strength/absence, cross-play handling)
the fairness/competitive-integrity line the team is willing to defend, stated explicitly and treated as contested where it is
the accessibility framing of aim assist as an input-parity feature, offered without stigma

title: Camera Control & Input
determines: the sensitivity model (single vs. per-axis H/V, ADS/zoom sensitivity, FOV-consistent "uniform aiming" scaling, per-device tuning, units exposed)
the invert defaults & requirement (Y-invert and X-invert offered and functional, sensible default)
the stick-vs-mouse look-shaping policy (stick ramp/curve type; mouse raw with no acceleration; smoothing/damping as optional low-latency polish)
the look-stick processing pipeline (dead-zone type/size distinct from the move stick, response curve shape)
the mouse raw-input + DPI + FOV interplay (counts-per-360, FOV-independent angular scaling)
turn-speed and snap-turn behavior (analog turn rate, VR snap-turn/comfort settings)
the automation-handoff rules (auto-center, auto-follow, assisted framing, lock-on yielding to raw player input)
the options menu surface (which sliders/toggles are mandatory vs. nice-to-have)

title: Combat & Action Input
determines: which combo grammar (strings/branches/launchers) fits a given action or fighting design and how it's taught
link/cancel window sizes and startup/active/recovery framing per move class (light/medium/heavy/special/launcher)
what cancels into what (whiff/hit/special/dash-cancel rules) and how cancel windows create risk/reward
the input-leniency stack for combat specifically (combo buffer, negative edge, simplified/shortcut motions, command-input recognition)
the button-count budget vs. move-count mapping (how many distinct moves a given input surface can express legibly)
the charge/hold-attack model (charge-and-release, hold-to-tier, charge-vs-mash) and the defensive-input timing model (parry/perfect-block/dodge i-frames, reactive vs. predictive)
where a given game/genre should sit on the depth-vs-reliability (execution-accessibility) axis, and how to keep skill in decisions rather than in fighting the parser
which failure mode (dropped inputs, stiff/cancel-less combat, inhuman precision, misfiring motions, over-lenient mush) a symptom maps to and its fix

title: Context-Sensitive & Contextual Controls
determines: the context-resolution model (which context cues — proximity, facing, look-target, held-item, state — select a contextual action, and how resolution is kept predictable)
the prompt-system design (glyph/highlight/label/reticle/diegetic cue that announces the resolved action before the press, and its timing/legibility requirements)
the disambiguation and priority scheme (explicit ranking for overlapping contexts, and the player-visible cue that communicates which one won)
the dedicated-vs-contextual split (which verbs must never ride a context button, especially reflex/urgent actions)
the interaction-richness ceiling a control scheme can support before it needs a second contextual input
how contextual controls interact with remapping (rebindable context buttons, disjoint-context sharing) and cross-platform prompt/cue parity

title: Control Feel & Responsiveness
determines: the tightness↔weight axis placement per action and per fantasy
the acceleration/stop curve shape (snap-to-max vs. ramp; start/stop frame counts; top speed)
the reversal/snappiness tuning (turnaround time; the punch of the core action)
the feedback-layer pairing (animation commitment + screenshake + hitstop + audio) that sells the raw input response
the input-to-response budget (how latency, ramp, and animation commitment are allocated against a felt-immediacy target)
the feel-tuning workflow (exposed parameters, kinesthetic iteration, when to trust numbers vs. hands)
feel-parity technique across stick/button/mouse devices

title: Control Scheme Design
determines: the action inventory and its frequency/urgency tagging (which actions are reflex-tier vs. deliberate-tier, per-second vs. per-encounter vs. rare)
the input-budget assignment (which physical control carries which action, and why — reachability without leaving the stick, ergonomic grouping, genre convention)
the chunking/grouping plan (which actions cluster into a single learnable chord vs. remain independent)
the convention-vs-deviation decision (when to follow genre-standard bindings and when a deviation earns its cost)
the modifier/context-layer strategy (hold-vs-tap, double-tap, trigger-as-shift, modes, radial/quick-select menus) and its latency/ambiguity cost budget
the scalability plan (which inputs are reserved at scheme-design time for the game's full, late-game action set, not just the tutorial's)
the default-preset set (Type A/B, southpaw/inverted, alternate layouts) and how many presets to ship versus deferring to full remap
the device-level default-scheme differences (controller vs. KBM vs. touch) at the design altitude, deferring device-parity tuning to the sibling report
the assumption that every default binding is rebindable, and what that implies for how the default is authored

title: Cross-Platform Control Parity
determines: which modalities (controller, KBM, touch) a game ships and what each is tuned to be good at rather than merely "supported"
the per-platform tuning stance for aim/movement (stick aim assist curve vs. raw mouse; virtual-stick/button sizing and dead zones for touch; per-device sensitivity/response curves)
the parity-vs-divergence regime per mechanic (identical mechanics for fairness/cross-play vs. deliberate per-device divergence for single-player feel)
the input-advantage handling in cross-play (input-based matchmaking/lobbies, aim-assist calibration, or accepting the asymmetry)
per-device scheme density and control-prompt/glyph adaptation across controller, KBM, and touch
the touch-specific adaptation plan (occlusion-safe layout, auto-actions, simplified vocabulary) when mobile is a target platform
the per-device remapping and accessibility touchpoints parity must preserve

title: Dead Zones, Sensitivity & Response Curves
determines: the dead-zone type (axial/per-axis, radial/magnitude, scaled inner-and-outer, angular) and typical size per stick/trigger
the response-curve shape (linear, exponential/power, dual-zone, custom) and how it trades near-center precision against edge speed
the sensitivity model (gain from deflection to speed/turn rate) as a dial distinct from the curve shape
whether look/turn acceleration (a ramp over sustained deflection) is used at all, and its ramp parameters
the trigger-processing spec (dead zone, curve, actuation point) for racing throttle/brake vs. shooter analog triggers
what settings are exposed to players (dead-zone type/size, curve type, sensitivity, acceleration on/off, per-axis, trigger curve) and their sensible defaults

title: Device Support & Hot-Swapping
determines: the active-device signal (detection, debouncing, and what consumes it — prompts, scheme)
the mid-session controller/KBM switching behavior (seamless prompt + scheme swap, anti-flicker)
the multiple-simultaneous-devices policy (controller+mouse merge vs. owned-and-separate multi-pad)
the local-multiplayer device-assignment model (per-slot ownership, join/leave flow, Player 1 determination, no shared-device leak)
the disconnect/reconnect protocol (pause + messaging, slot-holding, same-player-to-same-device re-pairing)
the platform-plumbing choice (XInput/RawInput/DirectInput/SDL/Steam Input/console pairing) and device-identity handling across reconnects

title: Gamepad / Controller Input
determines: the stick/trigger/bumper/face-button/d-pad assignment for a game's action set (which physical input class carries which action, and why)
which industry conventions the scheme must honor by default (left-move/right-look, A/Cross-confirm, B/Circle-cancel, triggers-fire/aim, bumpers-modify) and what justifies a deviation
the ergonomic frequency × reach mapping (which actions must sit under the resting thumb, which can live on the d-pad, which must never require leaving the stick)
the button-budget technique used to fit more actions than physical inputs (modifiers, context, hold-vs-tap, quick-slots) at the controller-specific altitude
the platform-glyph and hardware-extras plan (Xbox/DualSense/Switch prompt correctness; DualSense adaptive triggers/touchpad; Switch Joy-Con specifics; Elite/back-paddle treatment)
the comfort floor (no required uncomfortable simultaneous press, no critical action on L3/R3, no twitch action on the d-pad while steering)

title: Haptics, Rumble & Force Feedback
determines: the haptic hardware target per platform (ERM dual-motor rumble → LRA/HD Rumble → DualSense voice-coil actuators → adaptive triggers → force-feedback wheels/sticks) and what each tier can and cannot render
the rumble/texture design method (frequency choice — low thud vs. high buzz vs. fine texture — plus an attack/sustain/decay intensity envelope) mapped to concrete game events
the adaptive-trigger design method (variable resistance as feel AND mechanic — bowstring draw, weapon jam/break) and its graceful-fallback requirement on non-adaptive-trigger hardware
the force-feedback design method for wheels/sticks (deriving forces from physics/sim state — grip loss, kerb strikes, weight transfer) and how it differs from, and overlaps with, controller rumble

the haptics-as-information-channel method (distinct, learnable patterns → directional/threat pulses, state cadences, surface telegraphing) that reinforces a subtle visual/audio cue without ever being its sole carrier
the game-feel trinity timing rule (haptic pulse must land within the same frame/window as the visual and audio hit, not trail it) that keeps an impact feeling unified rather than mushy

the accessibility/opt-out contract every haptic feature must satisfy (tunable intensity, fully disable-able, graceful degradation on weaker/absent hardware, never the only carrier of critical information)

title: Input Buffering & Timing Windows
determines: which buffer types a game needs (jump buffer, attack/combo buffer, generic queued-action buffer, command-input buffer) and which actions get them
buffer window sizes (in frames-at-a-stated-rate and in milliseconds) per action and per genre
coyote-time sizing and where it applies (jump-off-ledge and its analogues: parry/dodge/interact grace)
the general leniency-window model (early/late acceptance) and how it differs from a buffer
the forgiving-vs-precise tuning dial placement per action, genre, and game speed
the latency-safety rule that keeps buffering from delaying a valid-now input
frame-rate-independent window implementation (time-based, not raw-frame-count-based)
where buffers/windows attach in the action-mapping/phase model (cross-ref architecture)
the negative-edge / input-priority / reversal-window leniency techniques and when they apply

title: Input Latency & Responsiveness
determines: the end-to-end latency budget (per-stage millisecond allocation from device to photon) for a target genre/platform
the measurement protocol (button-to-photon methodology, tooling, trial count/statistics) to validate a latency claim rather than guess it
the render-ahead / frames-in-flight policy and its trade-off against smoothness and GPU utilization
the engine input-read timing policy (where in the frame input is sampled)
the V-Sync/VRR/low-latency-mode policy per platform and genre
the device/poll-rate recommendation (wired vs. wireless, poll rate, display Game Mode guidance) surfaced to players
the reconciliation of intentional buffering latency against total input-to-photon budget
the genre-specific latency tolerance used to set "good enough" vs. "must optimize further"

title: Input Remapping & Rebinding
determines: what "full remap" requires (every action × any compatible input) versus the partial-remap failure pattern
which preset schemes to ship (southpaw, lefty, legacy, genre-standard) and how they're authored so a switch is one click
the conflict-detection and resolution policy (block / swap / warn / allow-in-disjoint-context) and what the player sees in each case
the per-device binding model (separate persisted binding sets per control scheme, auto-applied on hot-swap)
the remap UI/UX contract (live input-prompt capture, per-action labels, reset-to-default, discoverability, profile/cloud persistence)
how remapping functions as an accessibility baseline, and what a system must guarantee to not lock out a disabled player
the bindings data model (action-to-input maps, multiple bindings per action, serialization/versioning of a rebind file, absent-device handling)
the console-glyph / platform-cert requirements a shipped remap feature must satisfy

title: Input System Architecture
determines: the input pipeline's layer structure (raw OS input to device normalization to action mapping to gameplay-by-intent) and what lives in each layer
the polling/event split (what to poll per frame vs. what to capture as discrete events) and how to reconcile them without dropping sub-frame presses
the action-mapping model (actions, axes/values, phases/states, composite bindings, modifiers, per-scheme bindings)
the device-normalization approach (gamepad/KBM/touch behind one interface; where device differences legitimately leak through; control-scheme detection)
the input-context / action-map switching approach (gameplay/menu/vehicle layers; priority and consumption rules for conflict resolution)
which engine-native system to adopt or emulate (Unreal Enhanced Input, Unity Input System, Godot InputMap) given engine choice
the "gameplay never names a device" audit method and the abstraction-leak red flags to gate on before shipping

title: Keyboard & Mouse Input
determines: the mouse-aim signal chain (DPI/CPI × in-game sensitivity → turn rate) and the cm/360 measure used to report it portably
whether raw input is used (bypassing OS pointer acceleration/ballistics) and why it is a correctness requirement, not a preference
whether in-game mouse acceleration exists at all, and its default (off, or exposed and off-by-default)
the FOV-consistency policy (FOV-scaled / zoom / per-scope sensitivity) that keeps effective aim constant across zoom levels
the keybind layout (WASD anchor, home-row-neighborhood reach tiers, modifier usage) and the frequency/reach binding rule
the n-key-rollover / ghosting hardware floor a control scheme must not depend on exceeding, and the design implication for simultaneous-input schemes
the absolute-displacement (mouse) vs. rate (stick) input model and why the same game needs genuinely different aim schemes per device

which settings must be exposed to KBM players (sensitivity + cm/360 reference, raw-input toggle, acceleration toggle, FOV, per-scope sensitivity, polling-rate awareness, full rebinding) and sensible defaults

the KBM-vs-controller affordance trade-off (free high-resolution relative pointer and large discrete bind space vs. no analog key gradation and different ergonomics) that a cross-platform design must preserve per device

title: Motion & Gyro Controls
determines: whether to add gyro fine-aim as a layer on top of stick aim, and the stick+gyro division of labor (coarse vs. fine)
the gyro axis choice (yaw/roll/pitch), the world-vs-local space setting, and the sensitivity model for gyro
the calibration/recentering method (recenter button, hold-to-disable, drift correction) required before gyro ships
whether tilt/orientation control (steering, balancing) is offered, and whether it is default or optional
whether motion gestures (shake, point, swing, flick) are used for any action, and the reliability bar they must clear first
the opt-out/remap contract every motion feature must satisfy before it ships (never the only way to do a core action)
per-hardware defaults (Switch Joy-Con/Pro, DualSense, Steam Controller/Steam Deck, Wii Remote legacy, phone sensors)

title: Movement Controls & Character Control
determines: the movement model shape (state machine + physics/kinematics) and which variables to expose
the grippy↔momentum placement (precision platformer vs. flow/momentum vs. vehicle-weighted)
the acceleration/deceleration/turn-rate/friction tuning for ground locomotion
the air-control model (gravity, jump velocity, variable-height jump, air-steer strength, air friction)
the traversal-verb vocabulary (dash, double/wall-jump, wall-run, climb, grapple, vehicle moves) and how verbs compose and gate level design
the forgiveness layer (coyote time, jump buffering, edge-snap) that makes tight movement read as fair
the movement-diagnosis method (symptom → likely cause → dial) for fixing floaty/slippery/sluggish/dead-air-control movement

title: Specialized & Adaptive Controllers
determines: what a racing wheel/pedal set needs from the input system (rotation axis, force-feedback output, separate analog pedals, handbrake/shifter, per-axis calibration)
what a HOTAS/flight yoke/rudder-pedal setup needs (many freely bindable axes/hats/buttons, workable complex-sim defaults, per-device profiles)
what a fight/arcade stick needs (clean digital-stick + button-cluster mapping, SOCD handling/cleaning)

what adaptive hubs (Xbox Adaptive Controller, PlayStation Access) require the game to expose and never require (every action a remappable single input; no chords/simultaneous presses/mandatory holds-or-mashing)
what single switches, the QuadStick, eye-tracking, and voice need (single-input sufficiency, timing tolerance)
the detection/profile/calibration model that lets each device class keep its own saved bindings

title: Targeting & Lock-On Systems
determines: the soft-vs-hard lock-on model (bias-without-commitment vs. commit-and-orient; which the game needs and why)
the candidate-set rule (range + on-screen/frustum + line-of-sight gathering) feeding target selection
